content: Salpingitis is a condition characterized by infection and inflammation of the fallopian tubes. While the term is often used interchangeably with pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), it is important to note that PID is a broader term that encompasses various infections of the female upper genital tract, including endometritis (inflammation of the uterine lining), oophoritis (inflammation of the ovaries), myometritis (inflammation of the uterine muscle), parametritis (inflammation of the tissues surrounding the uterus), and infections of the pelvic peritoneum. In contrast, salpingitis specifically refers to the infection and inflammation localized to the fallopian tubes. In the United States, over one million cases of acute salpingitis are reported annually. However, the actual number of cases is likely higher due to underreporting, delays in diagnosis, and the fact that many cases are only identified after the condition has progressed to chronic complications. Among women aged 16 to 25, salpingitis is the most common serious infection, affecting approximately 11% of women of reproductive age. The condition is more prevalent among Black women and individuals from lower socioeconomic backgrounds. However, this increased incidence is thought to be associated with factors such as earlier initiation of sexual activity, having multiple sexual partners, and limited access to adequate healthcare, rather than being directly linked to race or socioeconomic status. The highest prevalence of salpingitis is observed in individuals aged 15 to 24, likely due to increased risk behaviors such as having multiple sexual partners, reduced awareness of symptoms, and lower rates of contraceptive use in this age group. Salpingitis can be classified into two types: acute and chronic. Acute salpingitis is characterized by redness and swelling of the fallopian tubes. The inner walls of the tubes may adhere to one another, leading to obstruction. In some cases, the fallopian tubes may also become attached to the surrounding intestinal structures. Chronic salpingitis, on the other hand, is a milder form of the condition with less pronounced symptoms. It often develops following an episode of acute salpingitis and tends to persist for a longer duration. Chronic salpingitis may lead to the formation of a hydrosalpinx, which is a fluid-filled dilation of the fallopian tube. The infection responsible for salpingitis typically originates in the vagina and ascends to the fallopian tubes. Due to the ability of the infection to spread through the lymphatic system, involvement of one fallopian tube often results in infection of the other tube as well. When diagnosing salpingitis, it is essential to differentiate it from other conditions that can cause similar symptoms, such as lower abdominal pain and fever. These conditions include appendicitis, diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease, cystitis, colorectal cancer, and endometritis.
